why: Every B2B deal ends with objections, a negotiation and a signature, and that is where margin is won or lost. Account executives and key account managers are hired to defend the price, trade concessions instead of giving them away, get through procurement and legal, and close on a date they can forecast.
outcome: handle objections with a method, answer the classic ones, compute what a discount really costs, prepare a negotiation (BATNA, ZOPA, target, walk-away, concessions), negotiate packages with “if… then…”, work with procurement and legal, close with a mutual action plan and learn from won and lost deals.

lessons.title: Objections: why they are good news, and a method
text: An objection is a buyer telling you what stands between them and a yes. Silence is worse: a prospect who raises no concern and does not buy has simply decided the discussion is not worth having. An objection means they are still engaged, picturing how your offer would work in their company, and giving you information you would not have had otherwise.

Most objections are not a final no. They fall into a few families: a real concern (the price is above budget, a feature is missing, the project looks risky), a misunderstanding (they think the setup takes six months when it takes six weeks), a stall (“send me something”, “call me next quarter”) that hides low interest or low priority, and a smokescreen that hides the real objection, often someone else’s opinion or a competitor already chosen. Your first job is to find out which one you face.

A reliable method has five steps. Listen to the end, without interrupting or preparing your reply. Clarify with an open question (“When you say expensive, compared with what?”) to understand the real issue. Isolate it: “Apart from the price, is there anything else that would stop you going ahead?”; if there are other concerns, you want them all on the table now, not one after the other. Answer the real concern with proof, a customer story or the buyer’s own figures, not with a speech. Confirm that the answer worked: “Does that address your concern on the timeline?”

Two habits help. Acknowledge before answering (“That’s a fair point, many finance teams ask the same”): it lowers the tension without agreeing that the objection is right. And answer with questions more than statements, because a buyer believes what they say themselves. The Sandler method goes further and asks the rep to raise the likely objections first (“At this stage people often worry about the migration; is that the case for you?”), which removes surprises at the end of the cycle.

In interviews, hiring managers often play an objection on the spot. They are not looking for a clever one-liner: they want to see you stay calm, ask a question and handle it in steps. Arguing, offering a discount at the first push, or talking for two minutes without checking are the classic mistakes, in interviews and in real deals.
points: An objection is information; silence, or “let me think about it” with no next step, is worse.
Find the type: real concern, misunderstanding, stall or smokescreen.
Method: listen, clarify, isolate, answer, confirm.
Acknowledge before answering; acknowledging is not agreeing.
Raise the likely objections yourself before the buyer does (Sandler).

example.code:
Buyer: Honestly, this looks expensive.
Rep:   Thanks for saying it now. When you say expensive, compared with what?        <- clarify
Buyer: Our current tool costs about half.
Rep:   Got it. Apart from the price, is there anything else that would stop you?  <- isolate
Buyer: No, the team liked the demo. It's really the budget.
Rep:   You told me the team loses about 6 hours a week on manual exports.
       At 47 weeks and 50 euros an hour, that's about 14,000 a year,
       more than the gap in price.                                                <- answer with their numbers
       Does that change how you see the cost?                                     <- confirm
Buyer: It does, if those hours are real. Can you show that to my CFO?
Rep:   Yes. Shall we book 30 minutes with her on Thursday?                        <- next step
example.note: Each line has one job. The answer reuses the buyer’s own figures from discovery, and the exchange ends on a dated next step.

lessons.title: The classic objections and model answers
text: The same six or seven objections come back in every sales job. Good teams write them down with tested first replies (an objection handling guide) so that a new rep does not improvise. A first reply is not a script to recite: it opens the conversation, and then the method of the previous lesson takes over (clarify, isolate, answer, confirm).

“It’s too expensive.” Do not defend the price and do not drop it. Ask what they compare it with (their budget, a competing offer, doing nothing) and bring the discussion back to value and to the cost of the problem they described in discovery. “We already have a supplier.” Good news: they already buy this kind of solution. Ask what works well and what they would change, and suggest comparing on the one point that matters most to them, without ever criticising the current supplier.

“I don’t have time.” On a cold call it is often a reflex. Respect it and ask for a short, precise slot: “Understood. Twenty seconds on why I’m calling, then you decide whether we talk again.” “Send me an e-mail.” Often a polite exit. Agree, then qualify: “Sure. So that I send something useful, what is your priority on this topic right now?”, and agree a date to discuss what you sent.

“I need to think about it.” Usually something is unclear, or someone else has to agree. Ask what exactly they need to think about, or who else is involved: “Of course. What would you want to be sure of before deciding?” “It’s not a priority right now.” Maybe true. Ask what the priorities are and whether your topic connects to one; if not, ask permission to come back at a precise moment (the budget cycle, the end of their current contract) and log it in the CRM.

Behind each objection is a question to answer, not an opponent to beat. If you cannot answer honestly (a missing feature, a real price gap), say so and show what you do offer: your credibility is worth more than one deal. And record objections in the CRM: patterns across many deals tell marketing and product what to fix.
points: Too expensive → compared with what? Bring it back to value and the cost of the problem.
We have a supplier → what works, what would you change? Never criticise the incumbent.
Send me an e-mail → agree, qualify the priority, fix a date to discuss it.
Need to think about it → about what exactly, and who else decides?
Not a priority → which priorities, and when should we talk again (logged in the CRM)?

example.code:
OBJECTION                 FIRST REPLY (then: clarify, isolate, answer, confirm)
------------------------  ------------------------------------------------------------
Too expensive             "Compared with what: your budget, another offer, or doing nothing?"
We have a supplier        "Good. What works well with them, and what would you improve?"
No time                   "Understood. 20 seconds on why I'm calling, then you decide."
Send me an e-mail         "Sure. What should it cover so it's useful to you?"
Need to think about it    "Of course. What would you want to be sure of first?"
Not a priority            "What is the priority this quarter? When should we talk again?"
example.note: One opening line per objection, as an objection handling guide shows it. The rest of the conversation follows the method.

lessons.title: Price and value: the real cost of a discount
text: Present the price after the value, never before: once the buyer has agreed on the problem, what it costs them and the result they expect. State the price clearly and once, in a calm voice, then stop talking. Rushing to justify it (“I know it’s a lot, but…”) tells the buyer you do not believe in it yourself.

A discount costs much more than it looks, because it comes straight out of the margin. On a €50,000 deal that costs €30,000 to deliver, the gross margin is €20,000. A 10 % discount removes €5,000: the price falls by 10 % but the margin falls by 25 %. This is why sales managers limit discounts and require approval above a threshold, through a discount grid or a deal desk.

To make up for a discount with volume, you need far more than the discount rate. With a 40 % gross margin and a 10 % discount, every 100 of list price now earns 30 instead of 40, so you need 40 / 30 = 1.33 times the volume: 33 % more sales just to earn the same margin. The general formula is volume needed = discount / (margin − discount).

There are better options than discounting. Change the scope (fewer users or modules, a pilot first); change the terms (a longer commitment, payment upfront, a case study or reference) in exchange for a lower price; or add something that costs you little but matters to them (training, onboarding help, a price lock at renewal). Any move on price should come with something in return; otherwise the buyer learns that pushing works and pushes again.

Watch the end-of-quarter habit: reps who discount to close in the last week train their customers to wait for the last week. Many companies set three levels: the list price, a floor that needs a manager’s or the deal desk’s approval, and a price nobody can go below. Know these levels before the meeting, not during it.
points: Present the price after the value, say it once, then stay silent.
A 10 % discount on a 40 % margin removes a quarter of the margin.
Volume needed = discount / (margin − discount).
Alternatives to discounting: trade price against scope, commitment, payment terms or a reference.
Know your approval levels (deal desk) before the meeting.

example.code:
A                     B
1  List price            50000
2  Cost to deliver       30000
3  Discount              10%
4  Margin before         =B1-B2            -> 20000
5  Net price             =B1*(1-B3)        -> 45000
6  Margin after          =B5-B2            -> 15000
7  Margin lost           =1-B6/B4          -> 25%
8  Volume needed         =B3/(B4/B1-B3)    -> 33%
example.note: The price falls by 10 % but the margin falls by 25 %, and you would need a third more deals to earn the same margin. B4/B1 is the margin rate (40 %).

lessons.title: Preparing a negotiation: BATNA, ZOPA, target and walk-away
text: Most negotiations are won or lost before the meeting. Preparing means writing down, for you and for the buyer, what each side wants, what each side can give, and what each side does if there is no deal. A rep who improvises gives away concessions nobody asked for.

The BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement, a term from Fisher and Ury’s “Getting to Yes”) is what you do if this deal fails: work other deals in your pipeline, keep the customer on its current contract, walk away. The buyer has one too: a competitor, building it in-house, or doing nothing. The stronger your BATNA, the less you need this particular deal. Estimate theirs, and strengthen yours by keeping a full pipeline.

Set three numbers before you meet: your opening, your target (ambitious but justifiable) and your walk-away point (below it, no deal; also called the reservation price). The ZOPA (zone of possible agreement) is the range between your walk-away point and the buyer’s: if you cannot go below €80,000 a year and they cannot go above €95,000, any deal will land in that €15,000 range. If the two ranges do not overlap, there is no ZOPA: change the scope, or walk away.

Anchoring: the first credible number on the table pulls the whole discussion towards it. Opening with your list price and the reasons for it sets the reference; letting the buyer open with “we have €40,000” sets a much lower one. Anchor high but credibly, with reasons, never with an absurd figure that breaks trust. If the buyer anchors first and far too low, do not negotiate from their number: re-anchor on the value and the scope.

Finally, list your tradeable concessions: what you can give that costs you little (training days, a price lock, a flexible start date) and what you will ask for in return (a longer contract, payment upfront, a case study, a faster signature, more users). Rank them by cost to you and value to them. In real deals this sheet is often missing, and the price becomes the only thing being negotiated.
points: BATNA: your best option if this deal fails; estimate the buyer’s too.
Opening, target and walk-away point are written before the meeting.
ZOPA: the range between your walk-away point and the buyer’s.
Anchoring: the first credible number pulls the discussion; anchor high, with reasons.
A list of tradeable concessions, ranked by cost to you and value to them.

example.code:
NEGOTIATION SHEET - Acme Logistics, 3-year platform deal

Our BATNA:    two other deals of similar size in negotiation; keep Acme on the 1-year pilot
Their BATNA:  in-house tool (6 months of work, 2 developers) or competitor X (cheaper, no API)
Opening:      110,000 EUR / year (list price, 3 years, 250 users)
Target:       98,000 EUR / year with a 3-year commitment and annual payment upfront
Walk-away:    85,000 EUR / year (deal desk floor); below that, offer a smaller scope

We can give (cost to us -> value to them)       We ask in return
- 2 extra training days      (low -> high)      - 3-year commitment
- price lock at renewal      (low -> medium)    - annual payment upfront
- start date in March        (none -> medium)   - signature before 30 June
- 5 % off year 1             (high -> medium)   - case study + reference call

Decision makers: COO (economic buyer), IT director (technical), procurement (terms)
example.note: One page, filled in before the meeting. The concessions are ranked, and each one faces something you ask in return.

lessons.title: At the table: concessions, packages and silence
text: The golden rule: never give a concession for free. Every move comes with a condition, stated first: “If you can commit to three years, then I can look at the annual price.” The “if… then…” form makes the condition clear, protects your margin and shows the buyer that every request has a price, which reduces the number of requests.

Make each concession smaller than the one before (decreasing concessions): 6 %, then 3 %, then 1 % tells the buyer you are reaching your limit; 5 %, 5 %, 5 % tells them to keep pushing. Do not split the difference by reflex, and do not give a last concession at the last minute without asking for something, such as the signature date.

Negotiate several issues together, as a package, rather than one after the other. When price, duration, payment terms and scope are discussed separately, each becomes a fight that one side wins. In a package you trade what matters less to you for what matters more, and both sides can come out better. One useful question: “If we solve the price, is everything else agreed?” It stops the buyer from opening a new issue after each concession.

Silence is a tool. After you state a price or make a proposal, stop talking and let the buyer answer; whoever fills the silence often gives something away. When the buyer makes a demand, do the same: pause, note it, and ask a question (“What makes 20 % the number?”) before you answer.

Stay calm and protect the relationship: you will work with this customer after the signature. Separate the people from the problem, and look at interests rather than positions: why do they want a lower price? A fixed budget line, a savings target, a competing offer? Summarise in writing what was agreed after each meeting. Fake deadlines or invented competing offers destroy trust once discovered; do not use them, and recognise them when they are used on you.
points: Never give a concession for free: “if you…, then I…”.
Decreasing concessions; never split the difference by reflex.
Negotiate a package of issues, not one issue at a time.
Ask “If we solve this, is everything else agreed?”
After a proposal, silence; then a written summary of what was agreed.

example.code:
Buyer: We need 20 % off to sign.
Rep:   (pause) What makes 20 % the number for you?
Buyer: Our budget for this year is fixed at 88,000.
Rep:   Understood. If we solve the budget, is everything else agreed: scope, start date, terms?
Buyer: Yes, the rest is fine.
Rep:   Then here is an option. If you commit to three years and pay annually upfront,
       then I can bring year 1 to 88,000, with years 2 and 3 at 98,000.
Buyer: Can you do 88,000 for all three years?
Rep:   Not on its own. If you also agree to a case study and a reference call,
       then I can take year 2 to 93,000. That is my final position.
       (silence)
example.note: The 20 % turns out to be a budget problem (an interest), solved with a package. Every move has a condition, and the second concession is smaller than the first.

lessons.title: Procurement, legal and timing
text: In mid-size and large companies, the person who chose your solution is not the one who signs. The purchasing department (procurement) joins near the end with its own goal, lower cost and lower risk, and is often measured on the savings it obtains. Plan for it: ask early in the cycle “How does purchasing work for a contract of this size? Who is involved, and how long does it usually take?” This is the paper process of MEDDPICC.

An RFP (request for proposal) is a formal tender: the buyer sends the same requirements to several suppliers and scores the answers on a grid. If you discover an RFP you did not help shape, your chances are low, because the requirements often reflect a competitor who was there before you. Decide whether to answer (fit, chances, effort) instead of answering everything; when you do, follow the format exactly and stay in touch with your champion.

Procurement negotiates price, payment terms, liability and contract terms. Payment terms have a cost: being paid at 90 days instead of 30 is credit you give the customer, worth roughly the deal value × your annual cost of money × the extra days / 365. In France the law caps payment terms between companies (in general 60 days from the invoice date, or 45 days end of month when agreed), so a request beyond that is not only expensive, it is not allowed.

Legal reviews the contract and sends redlines: proposed changes marked in the document (liability cap, termination rights, data protection, intellectual property, penalties). Do not negotiate legal clauses yourself beyond your authority: bring in your legal team, track every open point in a list with an owner and a date, and keep the signature date visible. Most redlines are routine; a few (unlimited liability, termination at any time without fees) change the value of the deal and go to your manager.

Timing matters on both sides. Vendors want to sign before the quarter end or year end, and buyers know it. Budget cycles matter too: money not committed before the customer’s year end may disappear, and many companies open new budgets in January. Use timing honestly: a real reason to sign by a date (a price increase on 1 July, a project start, onboarding capacity) is fair; an invented deadline is not.
points: Ask about the paper process early: who, which steps, how long.
An RFP you did not shape is often written for someone else: decide whether to answer.
Payment terms are credit: cost ≈ deal value × cost of money × extra days / 365.
Track redlines in a list with owners and dates; escalate the ones that change the deal.
Use real timing reasons (quarter end, budget cycle, price change), never invented ones.

example.code:
CONTRACT TRACKER - Acme Logistics (target signature: 28 June)

#  Clause            Their redline                Our position                 Owner      Status
1  Payment terms     90 days                      45 days end of month         Sales      agreed
2  Liability cap     unlimited                    12 months of fees            Legal      open
3  Termination       anytime, 30 days notice      for cause only in year 1     Legal      open
4  Data processing   their own DPA template       our DPA + their annex        Legal/DPO  agreed
5  Price increase    none over 3 years            capped at 3 % per year       Sales      open

Next call with procurement: 18 June, 10:00 (Sales + Legal)
example.note: Each open point has an owner, and the signature date is at the top. Clauses 2 and 3 change the risk of the deal: they go to the manager and legal, not to the rep alone.

lessons.title: Closing: trial closes, asking for the business, the mutual action plan
text: Closing is not a trick at the end; it is the result of a well-run cycle. When the pain, the value, the decision makers and the process are clear, the close is a natural next step. When a deal will not close, the cause is usually earlier: weak discovery, no access to the economic buyer, no reason to act now.

A trial close tests readiness along the way: “Based on what you’ve seen, does this solve the reporting problem?”, “If we start in March, does that work for your team?” A yes builds momentum; a no brings out an objection you can still handle. Use them after each important step, not only at the end.

The classic closing techniques, used honestly: the summary close (recap the problems, the solution and the value agreed, then ask for the decision), the assumptive close (talk about the next step as the natural one: “Who should receive the order form?”), and the alternative close (two options that are both a yes: “Do you prefer to start with 100 users or with the whole team?”). Pressure closes such as “this price is only valid today”, when it is not true, win a signature and lose a customer.

Above all, ask for the business. Many reps run good meetings and never clearly ask: “Are you ready to go ahead?”, “Can we sign by Friday?” Then stay silent. A clear no now is better than a deal that drags in the pipeline for months and spoils the forecast.

For complex deals, build a mutual action plan (also called a close plan) with your champion: every step from today to signature and go-live, with an owner on each side and a date (security review, legal review, purchasing, signature, kick-off). It turns “we’ll get back to you” into a shared calendar, shows early when a step slips, and helps the champion sell internally. Managers often ask to see it in forecast reviews.
points: Closing is the result of the whole cycle; a stuck deal usually has an earlier cause.
Trial closes along the way test readiness and bring objections out.
Summary close, assumptive close, alternative close; no false pressure.
Ask for the business clearly, then stay silent.
A mutual action plan lists every step to signature and go-live, with owners on both sides and dates.

example.code:
MUTUAL ACTION PLAN - Acme Logistics x our company
Goal: live before the peak season (1 September)

#  Step                              Owner (Acme / us)            Date      Status
1  Business case approved by COO     Claire M. / Sam (AE)         6 June    done
2  Security questionnaire            IT director / sales eng.     13 June   done
3  Legal review of the contract      Acme legal / our legal       20 June   in progress
4  Purchasing: PO and terms          Procurement / Sam            25 June   to do
5  Signature                         COO / our CRO                28 June   to do
6  Kick-off and onboarding plan      Hugo T. / CSM                3 July    to do
7  Go-live                           Hugo T. / CSM                1 Sept    to do
example.note: Built with the champion, working back from the customer’s goal. If step 3 slips, everyone sees that the 1 September go-live is at risk.

lessons.title: After the signature, and what lost deals teach
text: The sale does not end at signature. A clean handover to the customer success or delivery team protects the revenue you just won: what the customer bought and why, the results they expect, the people and their roles, everything promised during the cycle, and the risks. A customer who has to repeat everything they told sales starts the relationship with doubts.

Thank the champion and the decision makers, and set expectations for the first weeks. Agree early on what success will look like at 90 days: it is the base for the renewal and for any upsell. In many companies the account executive stays involved in the first months, especially on key accounts.

Lost deals are information. A win/loss review looks at won and lost deals with the same questions: why did they buy, or not? Against whom? At which stage did it change? What did we do well or badly? Ask the buyer directly when you can; buyers often say “price” first when the real reason was a weaker fit or a stronger relationship with a competitor.

Record the loss reason honestly in the CRM, with a short comment. “Price” on every lost deal tells management nothing; “lost to competitor X on API coverage, they needed a SAP connector” tells product and marketing what to do. Close lost deals instead of leaving them open: a pipeline full of dead deals makes the forecast wrong.

Keep the door open. Thank the buyer for their time, ask for feedback, and agree when to check in again, often a few months before the competitor’s contract comes up for renewal. Many deals are won on the second attempt, by the rep who left on good terms.
points: Handover: what was bought and why, promises, people, risks.
Agree the 90-day success criteria with the customer.
Win/loss review on won and lost deals, in the buyer’s own words.
A precise loss reason in the CRM; close dead deals.
Leave on good terms and note when to come back.

example.code:
HANDOVER NOTE - Acme Logistics (signed 28 June, 98,000 EUR / year, 3 years)

Why they bought:  6 h/week lost on manual exports; peak season in September
Success at 90 d:  exports automated for 3 warehouses; weekly report in under 10 min
People:           Claire M. (COO, economic buyer), Hugo T. (project lead, champion),
                  IT director (API access)
Promised:         2 extra training days; SAP connector "on the roadmap" (no date given)
Risks:            IT team busy until mid-July; procurement watches the renewal (cap 3 %)
Next:             kick-off 3 July (CSM + AE)
example.note: Everything the delivery team needs, including what was promised. The vague SAP connector promise is written down, so nobody discovers it at renewal time.

exercises.q: Excel on a real sheet: in B5, the gross margin in euros after the discount (list price, cost to deliver, discount rate).
exercises.hint: Net price = list price × (1 − discount); margin = net price − cost.
exercises.explain: 50000 × (1 − 0.1) − 30000 = 15000. The margin before the discount was 20,000: a 10 % discount removed 25 % of the margin. Pointing at B4 lets you test 5 % or 15 % at once.

exercises.q: In B4, the extra sales volume needed to earn the same margin after the discount (gross margin rate in B2, discount in B3).
exercises.explain: 0.1 / (0.4 − 0.1) = 0.333: 33 % more sales just to stand still. Show this to anyone who says “a small discount will bring more volume”.

exercises.q: A 3-year deal at the same list price each year, with a bigger discount in year 1. In B5, the total contract value (net of discounts).
exercises.hint: Add each year’s list price × (1 − its discount).
exercises.explain: 60000 × 0.8 + 60000 × 0.9 + 60000 × 1 = 48000 + 54000 + 60000 = 162000. A discount concentrated on year 1 costs less over the contract than the same discount on all three years (144,000 at 20 % each year).

exercises.q: The buyer wants 90-day payment terms instead of your standard 30. In B6, what this concession costs you (deal value, standard and requested days, annual cost of money).
exercises.hint: Cost ≈ deal value × annual cost of money × extra days / 365.
exercises.explain: 120000 × 0.08 × (90 − 30) / 365 ≈ 1578. Small next to the deal, but it is a real concession: trade it against something. In France the law also caps payment terms between companies, generally at 60 days from the invoice date or 45 days end of month.

exercises.q: Match each objection with the best first reply.
pairs: “Compared with what: your budget, another offer, or doing nothing?”
“Good. What works well with them, and what would you improve?”
“Sure. What should it cover so it’s useful to you?”
“Of course. What would you want to be sure of first?”
“What is the priority this quarter, and when should we talk again?”
exercises.answer: Each first reply is a question: it opens the conversation and finds the real issue before you answer anything.

exercises.q: Put the steps of handling an objection in order.
steps: Listen to the end without interrupting
Isolate: check there is no other concern
Answer the real concern with proof or the buyer’s own figures
Agree the next step with a date
exercises.answer: Listen, clarify, isolate, answer, confirm, then move the deal forward. Answering before clarifying means answering the wrong objection.

exercises.q: Sort these moves: tradeable concessions (good practice) or value killers.

groups.name: Tradeable concessions
items: Two extra training days in exchange for a 3-year commitment
A price lock at renewal against annual payment upfront
A later start date against a signature this month

groups.name: Value killers
items: 10 % off because the buyer said “too expensive” once
Splitting the difference without asking for anything
An extra discount after everything was agreed

exercises.answer: A concession is tradeable when it is given against something (“if… then…”) and costs you less than it is worth to the buyer. Value killers cut your margin and teach the buyer to keep pushing.

exercises.q: Your champion has chosen you. The deal is €98,000 a year for 3 years; your walk-away is €85,000. Procurement now takes over.

steps.text: Procurement opens: “We ask every supplier for 15 % off, it’s our policy.” Your first move?

choices.label: Ask what the 15 % is based on, and what else is open: budget, terms, scope
choices.feedback: You turn a position into interests and find out what you can trade.

choices.label: Accept 15 %: the champion wants the deal
choices.feedback: You give €14,700 a year for nothing, and procurement will ask for more.

choices.label: Refuse to discuss: the price is fixed
choices.feedback: Procurement must show a result; a flat refusal pushes them towards the competitor.

steps.text: They explain the budget line for this year is €85,000. What do you propose?

choices.label: If they commit to 3 years and pay annually upfront, then year 1 at €88,000, years 2 and 3 at €98,000
choices.feedback: A package with conditions: the budget problem is addressed and the contract value stays high.

choices.label: €85,000 for the 3 years, straight away
choices.feedback: You land on your walk-away point at once, with nothing left to give.

choices.label: Split the difference at €91,500
choices.feedback: Splitting by reflex, without asking for anything, shows that pushing works.

steps.text: Procurement accepts the structure but asks for 90-day payment terms.

choices.label: Explain you work at 45 days end of month, within the legal limit, and keep the package as it is
choices.feedback: Payment terms are credit; in France the law caps them between companies.

choices.label: Accept: it is only a question of timing
choices.feedback: 90 days is credit you give, and in France it is generally beyond the legal cap.

steps.text: Everything is agreed. On the final call procurement adds: “And 3 % more to close today.”

choices.label: Summarise the package, say it is your final position, and ask for the signature date
choices.feedback: A last-minute free concession would undo the whole structure.

choices.label: Give the 3 % to save the deal
choices.feedback: A concession at the last minute, for nothing, teaches procurement to do it again at renewal.

exercises.answer: Turn positions into interests, trade every concession with “if… then…”, keep payment terms within your rules and the law, and do not give a last free concession at the end.

exercises.q: Before a big renewal negotiation, what strengthens your BATNA most?
options: A full pipeline of other deals of similar size
A longer slide deck on the product’s features
A friendly relationship with the procurement manager
exercises.answer: Your BATNA is what you do if this deal fails. Other good deals in the pipeline mean you need this one less, so you can hold your walk-away point. A high opening is anchoring, not a BATNA.

exercises.q: The scope is agreed and your list price is €110,000. The buyer opens with “Our budget is €40,000.” What is the best response?
options: Re-anchor on value and scope: restate the problem, its cost and your price, then ask what the €40,000 is based on
Accept €40,000 and quietly reduce the scope
Say €40,000 is impossible and end the call
exercises.answer: Never negotiate from an anchor that is far too low. Bring the discussion back to value, then find out whether €40,000 is a real budget line (and change the scope openly) or a tactic.

exercises.q: Your walk-away point is €80,000 a year. You learn the buyer can go up to €95,000. How wide is the ZOPA, in euros?
exercises.answer: 95,000 − 80,000 = €15,000: any deal will land between €80,000 and €95,000. Your opening and your target decide where in that range.

exercises.q: You sell a 3-year SaaS contract at a list price of €60,000 a year. The buyer asks for 25 % off and 90-day payment terms. Prepare your negotiation sheet: both BATNAs, opening, target, walk-away point, tradeable concessions and what you ask in return.
exercises.answer: BATNA (us): the other deals in the pipeline this quarter; keep the customer on its current contract. BATNA (them): competitor X, or staying on spreadsheets (cost of the problem from discovery). Opening: €60,000 a year, 3 years, with the value recap. Target: about €54,000 a year (10 % off) against a 3-year commitment and annual payment upfront. Walk-away: the deal desk floor, e.g. €48,000 a year (20 % off); below that, propose a smaller scope instead of a lower price. Payment terms: our standard 45 days end of month (90 days is credit and, in France, generally beyond the legal cap). Concessions to give, ranked by cost to us: extra training days, a price lock at renewal, a flexible start date, then a bigger year-1 discount only. What we ask in return: 3-year commitment, payment upfront, a case study, signature by a date tied to the project start. Also: who signs and who in procurement and legal is involved, and the question “If we solve the price, is everything else agreed?”

interview.q: A prospect says “it’s too expensive”. What do you do?
interview.a: I don’t defend or drop the price straight away. I clarify: compared with what, their budget, a competitor, or doing nothing? I isolate: is price the only thing stopping them? Then I bring it back to the value and the cost of the problem in their own figures, and confirm it answers the concern. If there is a real budget limit, I change the scope or trade the price against a commitment, never a free discount.

interview.q: How do you prepare a negotiation?
interview.a: I write one page before the meeting: my BATNA and my estimate of theirs, my opening, target and walk-away point, the ZOPA if I can estimate it, the people involved and what each cares about, and a ranked list of tradeable concessions, each with what I ask in return. I also know my approval levels with the deal desk.

interview.q: When would you give a discount, and how?
interview.a: Only against something: a longer commitment, payment upfront, more volume, a case study or a signature by a real date, using “if…, then…”. I know what it costs: 10 % off on a 40 % margin removes a quarter of the margin and needs a third more volume to make up. Before discounting, I look at scope or added services that cost us less.

interview.q: What is a BATNA and how do you use it?
interview.a: Best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what I do if this deal fails. A strong one, mainly a full pipeline, lets me hold my walk-away point calmly. I also estimate the buyer’s BATNA, a competitor, building in-house or doing nothing, because it tells me how much room I really have.

interview.q: Procurement joins at the end and asks for 15 % off. How do you handle it?
interview.a: I expected them: I asked about the paper process early, so the timing is in the mutual action plan. I ask what the request is based on and what else is open, then negotiate a package with conditions, for example a lower first year against a 3-year commitment and payment upfront. I keep the champion informed and do not give anything for free at the last minute.

interview.q: How do you close? Give an example.
interview.a: Closing starts in discovery. Along the way I use trial closes, and for bigger deals I build a mutual action plan with the champion back from their go-live date. At the end I summarise the agreed problems and value and ask directly: “Are you ready to go ahead, can we sign by the 28th?”, then I stay silent. In my example, the plan showed the security review was late two weeks before quarter end, so we fixed it early.

interview.q: Tell me about a deal you lost. What did you learn?
interview.a: A strong answer names a real deal, the stage where it turned, the real reason (not just “price”), what you would do differently, such as reaching the economic buyer earlier or qualifying out sooner, and how you used it afterwards: a better discovery question, a change in your process, or a later win with the same account.

interview.q: How do you stop deals from slipping at the end of the quarter?
interview.a: By qualifying honestly before: a deal is in commit only when the economic buyer, the decision process and the paper process are known and the mutual action plan has dated steps. I check each step weekly and escalate early when one slips. I don’t buy the signature with a last-week discount; that trains customers to wait for the quarter end.
